title: Why weren't you Zusya?
hookLine: Reb Zusya feared being asked not why he wasn't Moses, but why he wasn't Zusya

cards: Scroll for thirty seconds and you'll find someone doing your life better. A better parent, a better runner, a better cook, a kinder friend, with better lighting.

You can measure yourself against all of them and come up short every time. Now picture an old Hasidic rebbe, much loved, on his deathbed. His students gather around him, and they're surprised to see that he's afraid.
He's crying. They ask him why. His answer has been passed from person to person ever since.

teach.b: The rebbe is Zusya of Hanipol, an early Hasidic teacher, a student of the Maggid of Mezritch, the Baal Shem Tov's successor.
He was known as a humble, joyful, often penniless man, so gentle that people told stories about his kindness. As the story goes, his students tried to comfort him.
Rebbe, you've been as faithful as Moses, as kind as Abraham. Surely you have nothing to fear.
And Zusya answered, roughly: when I get to the world to come, they won't ask me, Zusya, why weren't you Moses? They won't ask, why weren't you Abraham?
They'll ask me: Zusya, why weren't you Zusya? And what will I say? That's the whole story, and it turns the usual fear upside down.
The worry isn't failing to be someone greater. It's failing to be yourself: not a copy of Moses, but the whole of Zusya, with his own gifts and his own work.
In Jewish tradition every person is created in the image of God, and no two people are alike. Zusya takes that seriously.
In the story, there's a Zusya-shaped job in the world, and only Zusya can do it.
The story is mostly known through modern collections of Hasidic tales, and the exact words differ from teller to teller. But the question has lasted, because it travels so easily.

how: Reb Zusya's question is a widely quoted Hasidic saying, used by rabbis and teachers to encourage people to become fully themselves rather than copies of others.

o: the Baal Shem Tov's successor and chief student
a gentle Hasidic rebbe who feared not being himself
a Hasidic word for a humble, penniless student

games.q: what's inside the story — tap the pairs.

s: Zusya feared being asked why he wasn't Moses
he feared being asked why he wasn't Zusya.
Zusya was known for his humility and joy
people told stories about his gentleness.
Zusya's students tried to comfort him by comparing him to Moses
he answered that this wasn't the question he'd be asked.

games.q: you're one of Zusya's students. he's weeping on his deathbed. you tell him he was as faithful as Moses. what does he answer?
o: they'll ask why I wasn't Zusya.
I was never as good as Moses.
games.why: he said they won't ask why he wasn't Moses; they'll ask why he wasn't Zusya. and what will he say?

practice: Let go, for now, of someone you often compare yourself to. Instead, name one thing that's really yours: a kind of humor, a way of listening, something you notice that others miss, a skill your hands have.
Picture doing a little more of it, not to impress anyone, just to be a little more you.

wordCard.voice: Zusya, the Hasidic rebbe who on his deathbed feared not being asked why he wasn't Moses, but why he wasn't fully himself.

carryVoice: Your line: be Zusya. The question was never about Moses. That's day two hundred ninety-eight.

sources.ref: Hasidic tale attributed to Zusya of Hanipol
